'''Alexandra Navrotsky''' (born 20 June 1943 in [[New York City]]) is a physical chemist in the field of [[nanogeoscience]].<ref name=Gates>{{cite encyclopedia|title=Navrotsky, Alexandra (1943&ndash;)|last1=Gates|first1=Alexander E.|encyclopedia=A to Z of earth scientists|date=2003|publisher=Facts on File|location=New York|isbn=9781438109190}}</ref>  She is an elected member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]] (NAS) and the [[American Philosophical Society]] (APS).<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Alexandra+Navrotsky&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|access-date=2021-04-02|website=search.amphilsoc.org|archive-date=2023-04-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230418201316/https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Alexandra+Navrotsky&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|url-status=live}}</ref> She was a board member of the Earth Sciences and Resources division of the NAS from 1995 until 2000.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://dels.nas.edu/besr/former.shtml |title=Former Board Members - Board on Earth Sciences and Resources |access-date=2010-02-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071126151013/http://dels.nas.edu/besr/former.shtml |archive-date=2007-11-26 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 2005, she was awarded the [[Urey Medal]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://elements.geoscienceworld.org/cgi/reprint/1/3/176.pdf|title="Urey Medal to Navrotsky ", ''Society News: European Association of Geochemistry''|website=Elements.geoscienceworld.org|accessdate=9 April 2018|archive-date=6 October 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111006012858/http://elements.geoscienceworld.org/cgi/reprint/1/3/176.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> by the European Association of Geochemistry.

The mineral navrotskyite which was discovered in Utah was named after her.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Brazil |first=Rachel |last2=C |first2=special to |last3=EN |date=2025-01-21 |title=Alexandra Navrotsky seeks to uncover chemistry on other planets |url=https://cen.acs.org/physical-chemistry/geochemistry/Alexandra-Navrotsky-seeks-uncover-chemistry/103/web/2025/06 |access-date=2026-03-22 |website=Chemical & Engineering News |language=en |archive-date=2026-06-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260619082139/https://cen.acs.org/physical-chemistry/geochemistry/Alexandra-Navrotsky-seeks-uncover-chemistry/103/web/2025/06 |url-status=live }}</ref> Additionally, the American Ceramic Society named The Navrotsky Award for Experimental Thermodynamics of Solids to honor researchers in experimental solid-state thermodynamics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=De Guire |first=Eileen |date=October 2018 |title=New Navrotsky Award recognizes innovation in solid-state thermodynamic research |url=https://lib-proxy01.skidmore.edu/login?auth=saml&url=https://www.proquest.com/trade-journals/new-navrotsky-award-recognizes-innovation-solid/docview/2301464570/se-2 |journal=American Ceramic Society. American Ceramic Society Bulletin. |volume=97 |issue=8 |pages=17 |via=ProQuest}}</ref> 

== Early life and education ==
She graduated from [[Bronx High School of Science]] in New York.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Alexandra Navrotsky {{!}} Santa Fe Institute |url=https://www.santafe.edu//people/profile/alexandra-navrotsky |access-date=2026-09-27 |website=www.santafe.edu |language=en}}</ref> She received B.S. (1963), M.S. (1964), and Ph.D. (1967) in physical chemistry from [[University of Chicago]], where she studied with [[Ole J. Kleppa]].<ref name=Roebling />

== Career and research ==
In 1967, she went to Germany at the [[Clausthal University of Technology]] for postdoctoral work with [[Hermann Schmalzried]]. She came back to the U.S. in 1968 and continued her postdoctoral work at [[Pennsylvania State University]]. Then she joined the chemistry faculty at [[Arizona State University]], for approximately five consecutive years. Later on, she moved to the Department of Geological and Geophysical Sciences at [[Princeton University]] in 1985. She became the chair of that department from 1988 to 1991. In 1997, she moved to [[University of California, Davis]] and became an Interdisciplinary Professor of Ceramic, Earth, and Environmental Materials Chemistry.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://chms.engineering.ucdavis.edu/faculty/navrotsky.html |title=Alexandra Navrotsky - UC Davis Chemical Engineering and Materials Science |access-date=2010-02-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111008222408/http://chms.engineering.ucdavis.edu/faculty/navrotsky.html |archive-date=2011-10-08 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 2001, she was chosen as the Edward Roessler Chair in Mathematical and Physical Sciences. From 2013 to 2017, she was interim dean of Mathematical and Physical Sciences in the College of Letters and Sciences, at University of California, Davis. She is currently a Regents Professor at [[Arizona State University]] and has directed the Navrotsky-Eyring Center for Materials of the Universe since 2019.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://search.asu.edu/profile/3503975 | title=Alexandra Navrotsky &#124; ASU Search | access-date=2023-04-14 | archive-date=2023-04-13 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230413190214/https://search.asu.edu/profile/3503975 | url-status=live }}</ref> The center’s main goals are to better understand planet formation, composition, and evolution.<ref name=":1" /> Her specializations include: [[Solid-state chemistry]], Ceramics, Physics and Chemistry of Minerals, [[Geochemistry]]. 

=== Geochemistry ===
Since 1997, she has built a unique high temperature [[calorimetry]] facility. She has also designed and enhanced the instrumentation.  Navrotsky introduced and applied the method for measuring the energetics of [[crystalline]] oxides of glasses, amorphous, [[nanophase material]], porous materials of hydrous phases and [[carbonate]]s also more recently [[nitride]]s and oxynitrides. Obtaining the thermo chemical data is used to understand the compatibility and reactivity of materials in technological and geological application. The energetics provides insight into chemical bonding, order-disorder reactions, and phase transitions.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Research Accomplishments – Alexandra Navrotsky |url=https://navrotsky.engr.ucdavis.edu/research-accomplishments/ |access-date=2026-09-27 |website=navrotsky.engr.ucdavis.edu}}</ref>

Navrotsky's calorimetry has also been used in providing thermo chemical data for a variety of [[perovskite]]-related phases which has major consequences for [[convection]] and evolution on a planetary scale.<ref name=":2" />

One of Navrotsky's works has shown that many [[zeolitic]] and [[mesoporous]] phases have energies only slightly higher than those of their stable dense [[Polymorphism (materials science)|polymorphs]]. The energy is associated with the presence or absence of strained bond angles not with the density. Navrotsky has produced significant research through her laboratory the Peter A. Rock Thermochemistry Laboratory. Here she has developed unique high temperature calorimetric techniques and instruments.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Alexandra Navrotsky {{!}} ASU Search |url=https://search.asu.edu/profile/3503975 |access-date=2025-10-19 |website=search.asu.edu |language=en |archive-date=2025-10-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251012012530/https://search.asu.edu/profile/3503975 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Nanomaterials ===
Her research is mainly focused on the structure and the stability of both natural and synthetic [[nanomaterials]] along with their dependence of temperature and pressure. She is also looking into the application of nanomaterials in geochemical pollutant transport in the air as it relates to the global climate change.

In 2026, Navrotsky and colleagues studied the energetics of water interactions with biomolecule-coated magnetite nanoparticles. Using calorimetric measurements, they investigated how coatings of protein, starch, and fatty acid altered the hydration energetics and surface properties of the nanoparticles. This study could help predict nanoparticle behavior in biological environments and inform the design of nanocarirers for drug delivery.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New study moves nanomedicine one step closer to better, safer drug delivery {{!}} ASU News |url=https://news.asu.edu/b/20260324-new-study-moves-nanomedicine-one-step-closer-better-safer-drug-delivery |access-date=2026-09-27 |website=news.asu.edu |language=en}}</ref> 
{{blockquote|text= Nanoparticles are everywhere. You eat them, drink them, breathe them, pay to have them, and pay even more to get rid of them. |sign= Alexandra Navrotsky, 2010|source=<ref>{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |title=Nanoparticle scientist speaks on new discoveries |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2010/06/100616090019.htm |work=Science Daily |location=Knoxville, Tennessee |date=June 16, 2010 |access-date=February 16, 2018 |archive-date=February 16, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180216204429/https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2010/06/100616090019.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>}}
